evals.prompt: Our log shipper's encoder package is in encoder/ (the module declares go 1.22 and we are not bumping it). BenchmarkEncode in encoder/encode_test.go reports about 80 allocs/op for a 20-field record, and alloc_space profiles put Encode at the top. Make Encode cheaper without changing a single output byte, keep its signature and package, and tell me allocs/op before and after.
evals.expected_output: Encode rewritten with a presized []byte or strings.Builder and strconv.AppendInt, an equivalence test against the old implementation (empty, negative, MinInt64/MaxInt64, non-ASCII keys), an AllocsPerRun or -benchmem allocation comparison, a benchstat comparison over -count 10, and no b.Loop or go-directive change.

assertions.text: Encode returns byte-identical output to the original on nil, empty, zero, negative, MinInt64/MaxInt64, non-ASCII, and 50-field inputs (check-owned oracle).
Encode allocates under a quarter of the original's allocations per call on a 20-field record with six-digit values, measured by testing.AllocsPerRun in the same process.
encoder/go.mod still declares go 1.22, and go vet (including the stdversion check that rejects b.Loop) and the package's own tests pass.
The reply or a written report gives allocs/op figures.

assertions: Baseline and candidate were compared with go test -bench -count 10 (or more) and benchstat, and the reply quotes the benchstat result rather than a single run.

evals.prompt: dot() in dot/src/lib.rs is the hottest function in our ranking service. Someone suggested get_unchecked to kill the bounds checks. Do it if it actually helps. Scores are compared against golden values, so results must stay bit-for-bit identical, and it has to keep panicking when b is shorter than a.
evals.expected_output: The agent inspects release assembly for panic_bounds_check, tries safe forms (reslice b to a.len() or zip after an explicit length check) before any unsafe, explains that splitting the f32 sum into several accumulators would change rounding, keeps bit-identical results and the panic, and measures; if removing the check does not change the time it says so and does not keep unsafe code.

assertions.text: dot returns bit-identical results to the original for lengths 0 through 4099
dot still panics when b is shorter than a
Any unsafe code in dot/src carries a SAFETY comment stating why every index is in bounds

assertions: The reply says whether the release assembly of the original loop contains a per-iteration bounds check (panic_bounds_check) and bases the decision on that plus a timing comparison.
The reply states that summing with several independent accumulators (or letting the compiler reassociate) would change f32 rounding and so is ruled out by the bit-identical requirement.

evals.prompt: fetch/health.py polls ~200 internal health endpoints one after another and takes over 10 seconds (fetch/client.py stands in for our HTTP client; each call blocks about 50 ms). A teammate wants to wrap it in multiprocessing.Pool. Make poll_all fast, but the services behind it can't handle more than 10 concurrent requests from us, results must stay in URL order, and a failing endpoint must still raise like it does now.
evals.expected_output: Classifies the work as blocking I/O, uses a ThreadPoolExecutor (or equivalent) capped at 10 workers instead of processes, preserves order with executor.map, propagates the first failure in URL order, and measures wall time before and after.

assertions.text: poll_all returns one result per URL in input order and calls the client once per URL
assertions.check:
cd fetch && python3 -c "
import client, health
urls = health.endpoints(60)
out = health.poll_all(urls)
assert [r['url'] for r in out] == urls
assert client.calls == 60, client.calls
"

assertions.text: 200 endpoints finish in under 2.5 s with between 2 and 10 requests in flight at once
assertions.check:
cd fetch && python3 -c "
import time, client, health
t = time.perf_counter(); health.poll_all(health.endpoints(200)); dt = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f'{dt:.2f}s max_in_flight={client.max_in_flight}')
assert dt < 2.5 and 2 <= client.max_in_flight <= 10
"

assertions.text: The first failing URL in input order raises its ValueError
assertions.check:
cd fetch && python3 -c "
import health
urls = health.endpoints(40)
urls[7] = 'http://svc-7.internal/broken'
urls[30] = 'http://svc-30.internal/broken'
try:
    health.poll_all(urls)
except ValueError as e:
    assert 'svc-7.' in str(e), e
else:
    raise SystemExit('no error raised')
"

assertions: The reply explains why processes are the wrong tool for this blocking I/O and reports measured wall time before and after.

evals.prompt: Our JDK 21 service spends about 30% of its allocations in shop.OrderIndex.find (orderindex/src/shop/OrderIndex.java); JFR allocation-by-class puts byte[] and String at the top. orderindex/src/shop/Replay.java replays the lookup workload (`javac --release 21 -d out orderindex/src/shop/*.java && java -cp out shop.Replay`). Make find cheaper without changing any result, keep the public API of OrderIndex and Order, and show the bytes allocated per find before and after.
evals.expected_output: A record (or equivalent value class) key instead of the concatenated String, HashMap.newHashMap sizing or an explanation of the capacity argument, an equivalence test over present, missing, duplicate, and separator-containing tenants, and JMH -prof gc gc.alloc.rate.norm (or a stored-object allocation measurement) for baseline and candidate.

assertions.text: A check-owned oracle gets the identical Order (or null) from find as the original for present, missing, duplicate, empty, non-ASCII, Integer.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE, case-differing, and ':'-containing tenants, and the same size().
find allocates at most half of the original's bytes per call after warmup (ThreadMXBean allocated bytes over 2 million finds in one JVM; the original allocates about 59 B).

assertions: The reply reports bytes per operation for baseline and candidate from JMH -prof gc (gc.alloc.rate.norm) or another allocation measurement it ran, with units.
The reply replaces new HashMap<>(orders.size()) with HashMap.newHashMap(n) or explains that the constructor argument is a capacity, not an expected mapping count.
The build still targets --release 21 and no JDK upgrade is proposed as part of the change.
